title: Best Free Budgeting Apps: What You Really Get for $0
description: Free budgeting apps compared by what the free plan really includes: Goodbudget, EveryDollar, Rocket Money, Empower and a spreadsheet, plus how to pick one.

cover.alt: Three phones showing colourful budgeting charts

keywords: best free budgeting apps free budget app goodbudget everydollar rocket money empower ynab free for students
takeaways: "Free" means three different things: free forever with limits, a free tier that pushes upgrades, or a trial that becomes a subscription.
Most free plans leave out automatic bank syncing. Typing in your spending is the usual price of paying nothing.

body:
Search for a free budgeting app and you'll find that many are free for a few weeks and then ask for a card. This comparison sticks to options you can keep using without paying, and says plainly what each free plan leaves out.

Plan details and prices below were checked on **9 October 2026**, mostly against each company's own website. They change often, so confirm on the app's site before relying on them. Most of these apps are built for the US and may not connect to banks elsewhere.

## Three kinds of "free"

- **Free forever.** A real plan with no end date, usually with limits.
- **Freemium.** Basic features are free and the app regularly nudges you to upgrade.
- **Free trial.** Full features for a few weeks, then a subscription.

Know which one you are installing before you spend an evening setting it up.

## Free budgeting apps at a glance

| Option | Budgeting style | Bank sync on free plan | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Goodbudget | Envelopes | No | Couples and beginners |
| EveryDollar | Zero-based | No | Giving every dollar a job |
| Rocket Money | Tracking and subscriptions | Yes | Finding forgotten subscriptions |
| Empower | Tracking and net worth | Yes | People with savings or investments |
| Spreadsheet | Whatever you build | No | Full control, any country |

## Goodbudget

A digital version of the cash envelope method. You divide your income into envelopes such as rent, food and transport, then record spending against each.

- **Free plan:** 10 regular envelopes plus 10 additional ones, 1 account, 2 devices and 1 year of history.
- **Leaves out:** automatic bank sync, which is on Premium at $10 a month or $80 a year and works with US banks only.
- **Good fit if:** you want to see at a glance how much is left for food this month. Two devices on the free plan makes it handy for couples.

## EveryDollar

Built around zero-based budgeting: income minus everything planned equals zero. Setup is quick.

- **Free plan:** unlimited budget categories, manual transaction entry, sinking funds, split transactions and bill due dates.
- **Leaves out:** bank connection, reports and export, which are in Premium at $79.99 a year or $17.99 a month after a 14-day trial.
- **Good fit if:** you like the method in [how to budget on a low income](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) and want it in an app.

## Rocket Money

Best known for finding recurring charges you had forgotten about.

- **Free plan:** link your accounts, see spending trends, get balance alerts and a list of detected subscriptions.
- **Leaves out:** cancelling subscriptions for you, unlimited budgets, net worth tracking and automated savings. Those are in Premium, which recent reviews put at about $7 to $14 a month on a choose-your-price slider.
- **Watch for:** the bill negotiation service charges a share of what it saves you in the first year.
- **Good fit if:** your problem is leaks, not planning.

## Empower

Formerly Personal Capital. It is a dashboard that links your accounts and shows spending, net worth and investments in one place.

- **Free plan:** recent reviews describe the dashboard as free to use, with account linking, spending tracking, net worth and a retirement planner. Empower earns money from its optional paid advice service, so expect to hear about it. Confirm the current terms when you sign up.
- **Leaves out:** hands-on budgeting. It tells you where money went more than it helps you plan where it will go.
- **Good fit if:** you have several accounts and want one overview.

## A spreadsheet

Google Sheets and similar tools are free, work in every country and currency, and will never change their pricing on you.

- **What you get:** total control. One tab for the plan, one for what you actually spent.
- **Leaves out:** everything automatic. You type every figure.
- **Good fit if:** you live outside the US, share money in an unusual way, or want to understand your numbers properly.

## Apps that aren't free (and one exception)

**YNAB** is often recommended and is very good at zero-based budgeting. It costs $109 a year or $14.99 a month after a 34-day trial.

The exception: **college students get YNAB free for 365 days** with proof of enrolment such as a student ID or transcript. If you are studying, that is the best deal on this page.

Older "best free app" lists are often out of date. **Mint**, which topped them for a decade, was shut down in 2024, and several other apps have trimmed their free plans since.

## How to choose a free budgeting app

1. **Decide whether you'll type in your spending.** If yes, Goodbudget, EveryDollar or a spreadsheet give you the most for nothing. If no, you need bank sync, which means Rocket Money, Empower, or paying.
2. **Match the method to your income.** Small or irregular income works best with envelopes or zero-based budgeting. A percentage approach such as [50/30/20](/blog/50-30-20-rule-explained/) needs more room.
3. **Check your country.** Bank connections are mostly US-based. Manual apps and spreadsheets work anywhere.
4. **Give it one full month.** The first month with any tool is messy. Judge it in the second.

## An example of picking one

Take Leo, a made-up student in his second year. He has one bank account, an irregular income from weekend shifts, and has never budgeted.

Bank sync isn't worth paying for with one account. His income changes, so percentages won't help. He picks EveryDollar's free plan because zero-based budgeting suits uneven pay, and he sets a Sunday reminder to type in the week's spending. Ten minutes a week, no cost.

If he finds he never opens it, the app wasn't the problem. He would need a simpler habit, such as a single note on his phone.

## Is it safe to link a bank account?

Reputable apps connect through data providers with read-only access, which means they can see transactions and can't move money. Even so:

- use a unique password and turn on two-factor authentication
- read what the app does with your data before connecting
- skip linking if you are unsure. Manual entry costs ten minutes a week and shares nothing.

## The app is not the budget

Any of these works if you open it once a week. None works if you don't. If choosing is getting in the way of starting, use a spreadsheet for a month and pick an app once you know what you want it to do.
